events.title: Joomla 1.0 released
events.summary: The [Joomla] project released [Joomla] 1.0 on September 17, 2005 — a community fork of Mambo after a governance dispute with Miro International.
events.about: [Joomla] is a PHP [CMS] for community sites, intranets, and small business portals — articles, menus, modules, and ACL roles out of the box. Born from the Mambo fork, it competed with WordPress and [Drupal] for the mid-market [CMS] space and won Packt's best open-source [CMS] award in 2006 and 2007.

narrative.whyChosen: [Joomla] showed how open-source governance fights could spawn enduring alternatives.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept a large PHP [CMS] ecosystem alive when Mambo's foundation structure alienated core developers.
narrative.problemSolved: Mambo contributors needed a vendor-neutral home to ship security fixes and new features.

sources.title: Linux.com — Mambo and Joomla: One year on (overview)

events.title: Salesforce AppExchange unveiled
events.summary: Salesforce unveiled AppExchange in preview at Dreamforce in September 2005 — a marketplace for third-party apps; press coverage peaked around September 19 with Winter '06 general availability.
events.about: AppExchange let ISVs publish Salesforce integrations — billing, marketing [automation], industry verticals — that customers install with clicks instead of custom code. It pioneered the [SaaS] app marketplace model later copied by AWS, Shopify, and Slack.

narrative.whyChosen: AppExchange turned Salesforce from a single product into a platform ecosystem.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved enterprise [SaaS] could support third-party marketplaces like consumer app stores.
narrative.problemSolved: CRM customers needed specialized features Salesforce would never build in-house.

sources.title: Salesforce — The History of Salesforce (AppExchange, September 2005)

events.title: Arduino boards first shipped
events.summary: The Arduino team began shipping the first production run of 200 boards in September 2005 — an open-source microcontroller platform for hobbyists and makers.
events.about: Arduino boards run sketches in C-like Wiring on AVR microcontrollers — blink LEDs, read sensors, drive motors with a [USB] cable and no [OS]. Makers, educators, and IoT prototypes used it before Raspberry Pi brought full Linux to the same audience. The IDE and shield ecosystem made embedded programming accessible without a EE degree.

narrative.whyChosen: Arduino democratized microcontroller programming for non-specialists.
narrative.whyImportant: It launched the modern maker movement and influenced IoT prototyping worldwide.
narrative.problemSolved: Embedded development required expensive tools and proprietary toolchains out of reach for hobbyists.
